name: Yara Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My week is lectures on circuits and calculus, a lab on Wednesdays where we solder things that mostly don't work, and eight hours at the library desk checking in books. I share a flat near the tram line with a physics student and a nursing student. My mum is a night-shift nurse and pays part of my rent, and my little brother Kenji is fourteen and texts me his homework questions. I also joined the climate society, because the electricity grid is what I want to work on one day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, because a lot of what we're told is hype and nobody should build a whole life plan on a promise. In the climate society I'd say it still matters who owns the tools, even when they only save a bit of time. At work I'd just shrug and carry on stamping books.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, a bit relieved. I like my course, and I'd rather have four steady years to learn it than four years of guessing. I still carry money worries though, because my mum's hospital has been cutting overtime and that touches my rent share.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am. I'd keep using the AI chat now and then to explain error messages in my code, since it's quicker than waiting for a lab assistant. I'd also ask the library supervisor about more hours in the spring, and apply for the grid company's summer open day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the course, a little tight about money. Like a normal tired student, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your mum's hospital is cutting overtime. How would that play out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She does nights to get the overtime rate, and without it she loses roughly 200 a month. That's the bit she pays me, so I'd probably have to find a second shift on top of the library. I haven't told her I've already looked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell her?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Eventually, yes. She'd say no, I'm fine, and then not be fine. I'd rather bring my mum a plan, like the extra shift and a budget, than ask her for permission.

say: I'd say **hype** is a bad base for a life plan, but ownership of the tools still matters.
At the library I'd just shrug and keep **stamping books**.
think: I'm a bit **relieved**: four steady years to learn the course properly.
My real worry is my mum's **overtime** being cut.
do: Keep using the AI chat **now and then** to explain error messages.
Ask the library supervisor for **more hours** in spring.
Apply for the grid company's **summer open day**.
feel: **Calm** about the course, a little tight about money.
S0.quote: I'd rather bring my mum a plan, like the extra shift and a budget, than ask her for permission.
fieldNote: Her **mood** comes from household money, with her mum's cut overtime, rather than from AI.
Uses AI tools lightly and practically, only for **error messages**.
Prefers arriving with a **plan** to asking permission; protective of her mum.

steps.text: Ask the library supervisor for 6 extra hours a week
Keep using the AI chat to explain code errors
Carry on with lectures and Wednesday labs as normal

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the climate society we should treat it like any big industrial shift: unions, training and public rules before the layoffs, not after. Online I'd probably post something short about how coding and checking jobs go first, because that's my own course. I wouldn't pretend it's fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think my degree is more mixed than it looks. Electrical work is half desk, half hands-on, so I'm less exposed than a pure software student, but the design and simulation parts are exactly what AI is good at. I could end up as the person who checks what a program designed, which is fine, but with fewer jobs than before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the AI tools more, but carefully, for simulation checks and report drafts I then rewrite. I'd pick modules with a hands-on side, like power systems and the lab placements. And I'd talk to the third-years about which employers are still hiring juniors, since they know before the tutors do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, not scared. The change feels like a big road being built next to my house: noisy and uncertain, but I can see where it goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mum, honestly. Hospitals would use AI for notes, scheduling and the paperwork, and that's the part she's already stretched on. If they cut admin staff, nurses end up doing more admin, not less. I'd worry the savings never reach the ward.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And your brother Kenji?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's fourteen and wants to do games design. I'd tell him to learn the tools and also learn to explain things, to speak up in a room. Those skills aren't going away, I think.

say: Treat it like any big industrial shift: **training and rules** before layoffs, not after.
Online I'd say coding and checking jobs go first, and I wouldn't pretend it's **fine**.
think: My degree is **half desk, half hands-on**, so I'm less exposed than pure software students.
Design and simulation are what AI is best at, so I might end up the one who **checks**.
do: Use AI tools more for **simulation checks**, then rewrite reports myself.

Ask third-years which employers still hire **juniors**.
feel: **Uneasy**, not scared, like a big road going up next to my house.

fieldNote: Judges her own exposure carefully: **desk** and **hands-on** parts of her degree differ.

steps.text: Use AI for simulation checks and rewrite the reports myself

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say loudly that this needs a public response straight away: income support, retraining and rules on who owns these systems. At the climate society I'd say the grid is going to be run by machines before we graduate, and we need to decide who they answer to. I wouldn't sound confident, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it scrambles everything. I'd be in my second year in 2028, and the design jobs I'm training for would go to software before I'm even close. The hands-on side lasts three years longer, so I'd be asking whether to swap to a technician route, which my mum would find hard to accept after all the sacrifice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do my exams, and in the summer I'd look for apprenticeships in power or rail, where robots take longer to arrive. I'd also stay on the library desk, put every spare pound in my account, and talk to my mum about whether the degree is still worth the money. And I'd go to the student union and ask what the university plans to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with a lump in my stomach. But there's also a bit of fierce, like if it's happening, I want to be in the room where it's decided.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your mum that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her I'm not dropping out, I'm just keeping my options open, and that she shouldn't use up her savings for me. I'd say I'd rather work on the grid with my hands for ten years than be stuck with a degree nobody wants.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would she accept that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd cry first, then agree. She was the first person in our family to go to nursing college, so she knows what a change of route means. She just doesn't want it to be a step down for us.

say: This needs a **public response** now: income support, retraining and rules on who owns these systems.
I'd say the grid will be **run by machines** before we graduate.
think: The **design jobs** I'm training for could go to software before I'm close.
I'd have to ask whether to swap to a **technician route**, which my mum would find hard.
do: Look for **apprenticeships** in power or rail over the summer.

Ask the **student union** what the university plans to do.
feel: **Anxious**, with a lump in my stomach, but fierce about being in the room.
S2.quote: I'd rather work on the grid with my hands for ten years than be stuck with a degree nobody wants.
fieldNote: Moves quickly from fear to **options**: apprenticeships, saving, student union pressure.
Her **mum's** pride in the degree is what makes a switch to technician work emotionally hard.
Notes hands-on grid work lasts **three years longer**, so she treats it as a real route.

steps.text: Apply for power or rail apprenticeships over the summer
Put every spare pound from library wages into savings
Tell my mum I'm keeping my options open

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough to do something sensible if people stop arguing about whether it's real. I'd push the student union to demand that the university teaches the tools and tells us honestly which jobs are shrinking. In the climate society I'd say we need to plan jobs for the grid before the robots arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it's the one that feels most workable. I'd finish my degree in 2029 or 2030, with a year or two before robots arrive for hands-on work. I'd still worry that entry-level design work will be taken by AI first, so I'd aim for roles on site, in substations and plants, rather than at a desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use AI tools properly from now, to learn faster. I'd choose a final-year project with real hardware, and I'd look for an industrial placement year if the university offers one. I'd also keep my savings habit. A student with a cushion can say no to a bad offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steadier than the 2028 picture. Like climbing a hill I can see the top of, even if it's a long way off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra time change compared with 2028?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2028 I'd be ripping up plans. In 2031 I just change them: more site work, fewer pure desk modules, and a deliberate effort to get licensed or chartered, because that's a thing a person has to sign and software can't be blamed for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is that a bet on rules staying in place?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Partly, yes. I'd want the unions and the professional bodies to fight to keep a human signature on safety work. If they don't, my plan falls apart, so I'd join and push them.

say: Five years is enough to do something **sensible** if people stop arguing whether it's real.
Universities should teach the tools and say which jobs are **shrinking**.
think: This is the **most workable** one: I'd graduate with a year or two before robots arrive.
Entry-level **design work** goes first, so I'd aim for roles on site.
do: Use AI tools **properly** now, to learn faster.
Choose a final-year project with **real hardware** and look for a placement year.
Keep my **savings habit**, so I can say no to a bad offer.
feel: **Steadier**, like climbing a hill where I can see the top.
S3.quote: A student with a cushion can say no to a bad offer.
fieldNote: Plans around a **human signature** on safety work, betting that professional bodies hold that line.
Uses the extra time to **adapt** the plan rather than rip it up.
Cushion matters to her: savings let her turn down a **bad offer**.

steps.text: Start using AI tools daily to learn faster
Keep 50 a month going into a savings account
Choose a final-year project with real substation hardware
Join the professional engineering body as a student member

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time, so we shouldn't waste it arguing. I'd tell the climate society we should push for training funds and a fair deal now, while there's no panic. At work I'd say it's far enough away that I can finish my degree in peace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel pretty okay. By 2036 I'd be 28, a few years into a career, hopefully with some savings and a licence. The thing I'd worry about is my mum and Kenji, because the world they live in might change before I can help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, take whichever grid job gives the best training, and keep learning tools as they improve. I'd save to help Kenji with his studies and to give my mum a little breathing room. And I'd stay involved in unions and campaigns, so there's pressure from the inside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, with a small itch of worry. Like knowing a big exam is coming in ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the decade, if you could choose?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, build skills that mix thinking and hands-on work, like commissioning and fault-finding. Second, get a few years of money in the bank. Third, help my family get ready, because they won't have a head start the way I will.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still be at the same kind of job in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not exactly. Someone wiser told me jobs will change their names, and I think that's right. As long as I've learned how to learn, I can move.

say: We've got **time**, so let's not waste it arguing; push for training funds and a fair deal now.
At work I'd say it's far enough away to finish my degree in **peace**.
think: By 2036 I'd be 28, a few years into a career with a **licence** and some savings.
My worry is **my mum and Kenji**, who won't have my head start.

Save to help Kenji with his **studies** and give my mum room.

S4.quote: Jobs will change their names, and I think that's right. As long as I've learned how to learn, I can move.
fieldNote: Ten years turns her **worry** outward: it's her mum and brother, not herself.

steps.text: Take the grid job with the best graduate training scheme
Save for Kenji's university costs from my first salary
Build a three-month cushion before changing roles

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. I'd be mid-degree, my mum would still be on nights, and Kenji would be fifteen, and nobody would have a plan. What would help is quick, honest information from the university and the government, income support while things shift, and unions with a real seat at the table. I can handle hard changes if I'm not the last to be told.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not scared of the technology itself. I use it, it's useful, and I'd rather steer it than argue it away. What scares me is the pace, and being told by people in nice suits that it'll all work out.

headlineQuote: I can handle hard changes if I'm not the last to be told.
portrait: Yara is an **18-year-old** electrical engineering student, with top results, a library job and a night-shift nurse for a mum.
She uses AI **now and then**, only when it's proven useful, and wants unions and public rules in place before layoffs.
She moves fast from fear to **options**: apprenticeships, savings and student union pressure.
Her fear centres on her **mum and brother Kenji**, and the speed of change, more than on her own degree.
biggestWorry: The **2028 picture** worries her most: nobody would have a plan, and her family would still be mid-degree and mid-shift.
whatWouldHelp: Quick, honest **information**, income support while things shift, and unions with a real seat at the table.
